title: Portfolio Rebalancing: All at Once or Little by Little? | Dimensional
gist: Dimensional backtests 24 hypothetical 60/40 portfolios (Russell 3000 / Bloomberg US Aggregate, 1989-2025) that vary tolerance band (1/2/3%), rebalance end point (target vs. band edge) and trading speed (immediate, 5, 10 or 20 trading days). Trading speed made essentially no difference to returns (average best-worst gap of 4 bps annualized, mostly not statistically reliable) but slower trading cut turnover materially, especially with tight bands (7.1% to 4.7% one-way for a 1% rebalance-to-band portfolio), so rebalancing speed should be chosen on cost and turnover, not expected return.

themes.theme: Trading speed does not move returns

insights.claim: In a 1989-2025 backtest of hypothetical 60/40 portfolios (Russell 3000 equity, Bloomberg US Aggregate bonds), rebalancing immediately versus spreading trades over 5, 10 or 20 trading days produced no consistent return winner; the average gap in annualized compound return between the best and worst trading-speed variant was only 4 basis points.
insights.speaker: Matt Wicker
insights.so_what: Do not expect alpha from rushing or delaying a rebalance; the execution-speed choice for a balanced portfolio is a cost decision, not a return bet.
insights.quote: Across all groups, the average difference in annualized compound return between the best- and worst-performing trading speed portfolios was only 4 basis points.

insights.claim: Differences in average monthly return between 60/40 portfolios that rebalance at different speeds (immediate up to 20 trading days) are not statistically reliable in most cases, across 1%, 2% and 3% tolerance bands and both rebalance-to-target and rebalance-to-band end points.
insights.speaker: Matt Wicker
insights.so_what: Claims that a particular rebalance cadence or execution schedule adds return for a stock/bond mix should be treated skeptically absent statistical evidence.
insights.quote: the difference in average monthly return between portfolio pairs in each group is not statistically reliable in most cases

insights.claim: Dimensional concludes that the decision of how quickly to trade back to a target allocation should not be based on expectations of return differences, since speeds ranging from immediate to 20 trading days delivered similar returns.
insights.speaker: Matt Wicker
insights.so_what: Frame rebalancing execution policy around implementation cost, tax and turnover budgets rather than market-timing views on the rebalance window.
insights.quote: the decision of how quickly to rebalance back to target should not be based on expectations of return differences

insights.claim: Robustness checks with wider tolerance bands (2.5%, 5%, 10%), global equity and global fixed income indices, and portfolios receiving $5,000 quarterly cash contributions produced broadly similar observations to the core US 60/40 results, though with fewer rebalancing observations.
insights.speaker: Matt Wicker
insights.so_what: The speed-neutral-on-returns finding appears to generalize beyond US-only portfolios, though wide-band evidence is thinner because rebalances are rarer.

insights.claim: Average annualized one-way turnover in hypothetical 60/40 portfolios falls as rebalance trading is spread over more days, across every combination of tolerance band and end point tested over 1989-2025.
insights.speaker: Matt Wicker
insights.so_what: Spreading rebalance trades over days to weeks is a near-free lever for lower trading costs and, in taxable accounts, fewer realizations.

insights.claim: For a 60/40 portfolio that rebalances to the edge of a 1% tolerance band, average annualized one-way turnover dropped from 7.1% with immediate rebalancing to 4.7% when rebalancing over 20 trading days (1989-2025), roughly a one-third reduction.
insights.speaker: Matt Wicker
insights.so_what: Tight-band rebalancers stand to save the most turnover by slowing execution; quantify this against spreads and market impact in the policy.
insights.quote: average annualized one-way turnover decreases from 7.1% for immediate rebalance to 4.7% for rebalance over 20 trading days
insights.locator: Exhibit 2, Panel B: Rebalance to Band

insights.claim: The turnover savings from slower rebalance trading are largest when tolerance bands are tighter, because tighter bands trigger more frequent rebalances that natural market moves can partially undo.
insights.speaker: Matt Wicker
insights.so_what: Investors running tight drift limits should pair them with gradual execution; investors with wide bands gain less from slowing trades.

insights.claim: Trading a rebalance over a longer period reduces turnover because it gives natural market movement time to push the portfolio back toward target weights, and it lowers the risk of unnecessary back-and-forth trading in volatile markets.
insights.speaker: Matt Wicker
insights.so_what: In high-volatility regimes, immediate full rebalances risk whipsaw trading; staged execution acts as a built-in mean-reversion buffer.
insights.quote: lowers the risk of unnecessary back-and-forth trading in volatile markets

insights.claim: For investors able to spread trades out cost-effectively, a slower rebalancing approach may lower portfolio turnover without a significant impact on returns.
insights.speaker: Matt Wicker
insights.so_what: Advisors and multi-asset managers can adopt multi-day rebalance schedules as a default, provided per-trade fixed costs (commissions, tickets) do not offset the turnover savings.
insights.quote: applying a slower trading approach when rebalancing may lead to lower portfolio turnover without a significant impact on returns

insights.claim: Dimensional's study framework varies three rebalancing dimensions: tolerance band size (1%, 2% or 3%), rebalance end point (back to 60/40 target or to the nearest breached band edge), and trading speed (immediate, 5, 10 or 20 trading days), yielding 24 portfolios.
insights.speaker: Matt Wicker
insights.so_what: A usable checklist for specifying a rebalancing policy: define the trigger, the destination and the execution pace separately.

insights.claim: Multi-day rebalancing in the study trades each day an amount equal to the remaining distance to the end point divided by planned days left, measured from beginning-of-day weights, so it trades more if markets push the portfolio further away and less if they move it closer, ending early once weights are within 10 bps of the end point.
insights.speaker: Matt Wicker
insights.so_what: A simple adaptive schedule (e.g., 1.50% gap over 5 days = 0.30% on day one) that practitioners can replicate to capture the turnover savings.

insights.claim: For tax-sensitive investors, it may be better to rebalance all the way back to target weights rather than to the band edge when that can be done tax-efficiently, despite higher turnover, because a tax-efficient rebalancing opportunity may not recur soon.
insights.speaker: Matt Wicker
insights.so_what: Turnover minimization is not always optimal in taxable accounts; opportunistically use loss harvests or cash flows to reset fully to target.
insights.quote: the opportunity to rebalance tax efficiently may not come again soon

insights.claim: Rebalancing costs include explicit costs such as brokerage commissions, custody and exchange fees and taxes, and implicit costs such as bid-ask spreads and market impact; all else equal, more frequent rebalancing reduces drift from target but raises these costs.
insights.speaker: Matt Wicker
insights.so_what: The rebalance-speed choice should be evaluated against the specific cost stack of the account, since turnover savings only matter through these cost channels.

source_meta.author: Matt Wicker, CFA, Researcher and Vice President
